description: The core paradigms for designing algorithms and the mathematics for proving how fast and how correct they are: divide and conquer, dynamic programming, greedy methods, graph and flow algorithms, NP-completeness, and randomised and approximation methods. In the lab students step through each algorithm, plot growth rates, and measure running time against the predicted bound.
modelledOn: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, Introduction to Algorithms
outcomes: Analyse the running time and space of an algorithm using asymptotic notation, recurrences and amortised analysis.
Choose and apply divide and conquer, dynamic programming or a greedy strategy to a new problem and prove it correct.
Solve shortest-path, spanning-tree, matching and maximum-flow problems and justify the choice of algorithm.
Prove a problem NP-complete by a polynomial-time reduction and recognise intractable problems in practice.
Design and analyse randomised and approximation algorithms with stated expected-time or approximation guarantees.
Compare predicted and measured performance and explain any gap.

units.title: Foundations of algorithm analysis
topics: The RAM model, input size, and worst-case, average-case and best-case analysis
Big-O, Omega, Theta and little-o: definitions, proofs from the definition, growth-rate ordering
Analysing loops and nested loops; common summations
Solving recurrences: substitution method and recursion trees
The master theorem and when it does not apply
Amortised analysis: aggregate, accounting and potential methods on dynamic arrays and binary counters

units.title: Divide and conquer
topics: Merge sort and counting inversions
Quicksort with random pivots and its expected running time
Linear-time selection with median of medians
Integer multiplication by Karatsuba and fast matrix multiplication with seven products
Closest pair of points in the plane

units.title: Dynamic programming
topics: Optimal substructure and overlapping subproblems; memoisation versus tabulation
Longest common subsequence and edit distance
0/1 knapsack and pseudo-polynomial time
Matrix-chain multiplication and optimal binary search trees
Shortest paths by dynamic programming: Bellman-Ford and DAG paths
Reconstructing solutions and reducing space

units.title: Greedy algorithms and matroids
topics: The greedy-choice property and exchange arguments; interval scheduling
Huffman coding and optimal prefix codes
Minimum spanning trees: the cut property, Kruskal and Prim
Matroids and the greedy algorithm on weighted independence systems
Dijkstra's algorithm: correctness and priority-queue implementations

units.title: Graph algorithms and network flow
topics: Breadth-first and depth-first search, topological sort, strongly connected components
All-pairs shortest paths: Floyd-Warshall and reweighting for sparse graphs
Maximum flow: residual graphs, augmenting paths, shortest-augmenting-path analysis, max-flow min-cut theorem
Bipartite matching, edge-disjoint paths and other reductions to flow
Union-find with path compression and union by rank

units.title: NP-completeness and reductions
topics: The classes P and NP, certificates and polynomial-time verification
Polynomial-time reductions and what they prove
Satisfiability as the first NP-complete problem; 3-SAT
Classic reductions: independent set, vertex cover, clique, Hamiltonian cycle, subset sum
Coping with hardness: backtracking, branch and bound, parameterised ideas, SAT solvers

units.title: Randomised and approximation algorithms
topics: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo algorithms; random contraction for minimum cut
Universal hashing and expected-case guarantees
Randomised primality testing and error amplification
Approximation ratios; a 2-approximation for vertex cover
Metric travelling salesman: the double-tree 2-approximation and its tightness
Greedy set cover with ratio ln n; a fully polynomial approximation scheme for knapsack

units.title: Lower bounds and algorithm engineering
topics: The comparison-sorting lower bound with decision trees
Adversary arguments and information-theoretic bounds
Empirical analysis: fitting measured times to predicted growth, constant factors and cache effects
Choosing a paradigm: a short design project on a transport, market or mobile-money routing problem

schedule.title: Asymptotic analysis
schedule.exercise: Prove from the definition that 3n^2 + 10n is Theta(n^2), rank twelve functions by growth rate, and count the basic operations of a triple nested loop exactly.

tasks.title: Plot n, n log n, n^2, 2^n and n! on log axes for n up to 30 and read off the order of growth for each
Step through insertion sort on sorted, reversed and random arrays of size 16 and tabulate comparisons against the best, average and worst-case formulas
Time linear search, binary search and a nested-loop pair counter for doubling input sizes, then fit each curve and state the estimated order

schedule.title: Recurrences and amortised analysis
schedule.exercise: Solve T(n) = 3T(n/2) + n by recursion tree and by the master theorem, then compute the amortised cost of n increments of a binary counter with the potential method.

tasks.title: Apply the master theorem to six given recurrences, plot each solution against its predicted growth, and note which case applies
Count operations of a recursive algorithm for n = 2 to 1024, tabulate the counts, and verify them against the closed-form solution you derived by recursion tree
Trace 33 appends to a doubling dynamic array, plot the cumulative copy cost, and show the accounting-method charge that keeps the credit non-negative

schedule.title: Divide and conquer
schedule.exercise: Write the recurrence for merge sort and for the closest-pair algorithm, argue why the combine step is linear, and show where quicksort with a fixed pivot goes quadratic.

tasks.title: Step through merge sort on 12 numbers, record the recursion tree, and count the inversions found during each merge
Implement quicksort with first-element and random pivots, run both on 2000 sorted inputs, and compare comparison counts and variance
Implement closest pair of points by divide and conquer, test it on 500 random points against the brute-force answer, and plot the speed-up

schedule.title: Dynamic programming foundations
schedule.exercise: Define the subproblems and recurrence for edit distance between two words, fill the table by hand, and explain why the 0/1 knapsack table is not polynomial in the input length.

tasks.title: Compare naive recursion with memoised recursion for Fibonacci(30) and count the calls made by each
Fill the edit-distance table for two given words step by step and trace back the optimal sequence of edits
Solve a 0/1 knapsack for choosing market stalls under a budget, then scale the weights by 1000 and measure how table size and time grow

schedule.title: Dynamic programming on structures
schedule.exercise: Find the optimal parenthesisation of a chain of five matrices, run Bellman-Ford by hand on a six-node graph with a negative edge, and describe a rolling-array trick for LCS.

tasks.title: Fill the matrix-chain cost table for four matrices with given dimensions and read off the best multiplication order
Run Bellman-Ford on a 7-node graph with a negative edge, record distances after each round, and detect a planted negative cycle
Implement longest common subsequence with the full table and with two rows, reconstruct the answer in both, and compare memory use on 5000-character strings

schedule.title: Greedy algorithms and matroids
schedule.exercise: Give an exchange argument for earliest-finish-time interval scheduling, show a counterexample where greedy fails for coin change, and verify that the forests of a graph form a matroid.

tasks.title: Build a Huffman tree for a 6-letter frequency table, list the codes, and compute the saving against a fixed 3-bit code
Run Kruskal and Prim on the same 9-node weighted road network, compare the order edges are added, and confirm both trees have equal weight
Test the greedy rule on a given weighted independence system by brute force and report whether the exchange property holds or find a violating pair

schedule.title: Graph traversal, all-pairs paths and union-find
schedule.exercise: Compute a topological order and the strongly connected components of a task-dependency graph, then run Floyd-Warshall by hand on a four-node graph for two values of k.

tasks.title: Run breadth-first and depth-first search from the same node of a 10-node graph and record discovery and finish times for every vertex
Step through Floyd-Warshall on a 6-town road graph and show the distance matrix after each choice of intermediate node
Implement union-find with and without path compression, run 100000 random unions and finds, and plot the average find depth for each version

schedule.title: Maximum flow and matching
schedule.exercise: Find a maximum flow in a small network, exhibit the minimum cut with equal capacity, and model assigning five nurses to five shifts as bipartite matching.

tasks.title: Run augmenting-path max flow on a 6-node network, draw the residual graph after each path, and report the final flow value
Find the minimum cut of a given network from the final residual graph and verify that its capacity equals the maximum flow
Model assigning 8 drivers to 8 delivery routes as a flow problem, solve it in code, and check the result against brute-force matching

schedule.title: P, NP and polynomial reductions
schedule.exercise: Write a polynomial-time verifier for Hamiltonian cycle, reduce 3-SAT to a graph problem on a tiny formula, and explain what a polynomial reduction does and does not prove.

tasks.title: Write a verifier that checks a proposed certificate for subset sum and for graph colouring, and test it on valid and invalid certificates
Evaluate all assignments of a 4-variable 3-SAT formula in the logic tool, list the satisfying ones, and add a clause that makes it unsatisfiable
Implement the reduction from 3-SAT to independent set, convert 5 formulas, and check satisfiability of each formula agrees with the graph answer

schedule.title: NP-complete problems and coping with hardness
schedule.exercise: Chain the reductions independent set to vertex cover to clique, and decide whether a given scheduling problem is likely tractable or NP-hard, with a justification.

tasks.title: Find a minimum vertex cover of a 9-node graph by exhaustive search and show its complement is a maximum independent set
Implement backtracking for graph colouring with pruning, count nodes explored against plain enumeration on 12-node graphs, and report the saving
Measure the running time of exact subset sum for n from 10 to 28, plot the exponential growth, and estimate the largest n solvable in one second

schedule.title: Randomised algorithms
schedule.exercise: Compute the probability that random contraction finds a minimum cut, say how many repetitions give error below 1 percent, and show why universal hashing beats a fixed hash function on adversarial keys.

tasks.title: Simulate randomised quicksort pivot choices 10000 times with Monte Carlo and plot the distribution of comparison counts for n = 100
Insert adversarial keys into a fixed-hash table and a universal-hash table, and compare the longest chain lengths over 20 random hash choices
Implement a randomised primality test, check it on primes and Carmichael numbers, and measure the error rate as the number of rounds grows

schedule.title: Approximation algorithms
schedule.exercise: Prove that the matching-based vertex cover is within factor 2 of optimal, and build a bad instance for greedy set cover to show the ln n factor is tight.

tasks.title: Run the maximal-matching vertex cover on three graphs, compare each cover size with the optimum found by search, and confirm ratio at most 2
Build a minimum spanning tree on 10 points, take the double-tree tour, and compare its length with the optimal tour from search
Implement greedy set cover for placing mobile-money agents to cover villages, compare with the optimum on 8 small instances, and report the ratios

schedule.title: Lower bounds and algorithm design project
schedule.exercise: Draw the decision tree for sorting three elements, derive the log2(n!) bound, and write a one-page design memo that picks and justifies a paradigm for a routing problem.

tasks.title: Plot log2(n!) against n log2 n for n up to 100 and compare with the comparison counts of merge sort on random inputs
Time three sorting implementations on arrays of sizes 1000 to 1000000, fit each to its predicted growth, and explain the constant-factor gap
Choose and implement an algorithm for assigning minibus routes to depots under a capacity limit, prove its bound, and compare with a brute-force optimum
